lugubrious

loo-GOO-bree-us · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Lugubrious is looking or sounding sad, dismal, or mournful, often to an exaggerated or theatrical degree.

The funeral director's lugubrious tone, drawn out and heavy with sighs, made even the caterers feel like they should whisper.

Worked Example

The talk-show host put on his most lugubrious expression, sighing dramatically before announcing -- to nobody's surprise -- that the show's ratings had dropped again.

Lugubrious mournfulness is often so exaggerated or theatrical that it borders on comic, unlike quiet, sincere sadness.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

funereal: Funereal means suited to a funeral: slow, hushed, solemn, dignified. A funereal tone is genuinely grave and fits the occasion it marks. Lugubrious takes the same gloom and overdoes it -- the sadness is laid on so thick and theatrical that it can tip toward comedy.

dismal: Dismal means depressingly bleak or dreary -- dismal weather, a dismal report card -- and it describes situations more than performances. Lugubrious is gloom worn on the outside, in a face or a voice, usually exaggerated until it looks or sounds staged.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

buoyant: cheerful and optimistic

breezy: light-hearted and cheerfully casual

Where it sits · how deep the gloom appears — somber → lugubrious → mournful

somber vs. lugubrious: A somber mood is quiet, sincere seriousness -- subdued and respectful -- while lugubrious gloom goes further, laid on thick and drawn out until it turns theatrical.

mournful vs. lugubrious: Genuine, deep mournfulness comes from real grief, without any of lugubrious's theatrical edge.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — lugubri

Root — lugubri: mournful (from Latin lugubris, built on lugere, 'to mourn')

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of (Latin -osus)

Put it together

Put it together: Lugubrious combines lugubri ("mournful," from Latin lugubris, built on lugere, "to mourn") + -ous ("full of") -- literally "full of mourning," often stretched to a theatrical degree.

Where it comes from

Where it comes from: Latin lugere, 'to mourn,' sits inside lugubrious, which is why the word means more than sad: it is 'full of' mourning, grief worn openly and usually overdone. Even the word's slow, heavy sound fits the theatrical gloom it describes.
